newsitem.title: EL SALVADOR: El Salvador Congress OKs telephone privatization.
newsitem.headline: El Salvador Congress OKs telephone privatization.

text.p: El Salvador's legislative Assembly on Thursday approved a privatization law clearing the way to divide the state-owned telephone monopoly known as ANTEL into two companies that will be sold.
The vote was 47 to 37, with six opposition legislators joining 41 from the ruling National Republican Alliance (ARENA) in approving the deal.
Foreign and national investors, called "strategic partners" under the law, would be allowed to hold up to a 50 percent stake in each of the two new companies.
Of the other half, ANTEL workers can own up to 10 percent of each company with the remaining 40 percent of each new company being offered to retail investors in an auction of shares.
Opposition legislators objected to what they called a lack of discussion, alleging that the pro-business ARENA wanted to turn over the company to an unspecified "powerful financial group."
"We deputies didn't even see a draft of the law until today," Julio Regalado of the Social Christian Renovation Movement said during the two-hour debate before the vote.

Another deputy, Dagoberto Gutierrez of the leftist Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front (FMLN), accused the ruling party of engineering a "secret privatization" and warned of a "politically dangerous situation."
According to government statistics, ANTEL generated profits of more than 500 million colones ($57.5 million) in 1995.
ANTEL will be split in two in order to promote competition, backers of the law said.
About 50 ANTEL workers opposed to privatization protested the law from within the Legislative Assembly building, but did not interrupt the session.
Workers said they would launch an 18-hour strike immediately and threatened to escalate their protests.
